content.title: WNBA Draft: Why more rookies than ever will stick with their teams under the new CBA
content.text: PHOENIX — The cut-down date in the WNBA has always been brutal. Only about half of the rookies drafted a mere three weeks prior make it to opening day. Even a reigning Naismith winner, who has since won a WNBA championship, was cut ahead of her rookie year.It should become a thing of the past under the new collective bargaining agreement (CBA) that the Board of Governors and players union ratified last month. The long-term sheet and finalized document are still in progress.AdvertisementOne of the major wins for both sides is the introduction of up to two developmental players per team, which do not count against the salary cap, and the guaranteed mandate of 12 rostered players per team. Previously, franchises could and typically did carry 11 to pay individuals more under the $1.5 million cap.It’s not quite the roster expansion players yearned for, but it does begin to improve the player health and safety aspect of smaller rosters. The league is also expanding again this year with Portland and Toronto joining the fold. Teams in Cleveland, Detroit and Philadelphia will come on board through 2030.It adds up to more roster spots for mid-tier salaried veterans and draftees, a boon for the league that is successfully building up its college-to-pro pipeline while leveraging the marketability of headline college talent. And it’s a relief for fans that the names called at the WNBA collegiate draft on Monday (7 p.m. ET) will stick around longer than the three weeks before tip-off on May 8.AdvertisementIn total, the league will be at 210 players in the upcoming season after the new collective bargaining agreement (CBA) and expansion. That’s up from 144, not including those on short-term or hardship contracts, as recently as two seasons ago. There are at least 54 new spots for draftees to land. The three-round draft consists of 45 selections.The incoming rookies will also see more money in their bank accounts with accelerated opportunities. The No. 1 overall pick will earn $500,000 in salary, up from the $78,831 that Paige Bueckers made as a rookie in Dallas last year. After years of certainty, the top pick this year remains unclear. UConn senior shooting guard Azzi Fudd, TCU point guard Olivia Miles and Spanish center Awa Fam have all slotted into the top spot over the last month.The second pick will receive $466,913, the third $436,016, and all the way down to $289,133 for the last seven picks of the first round. Those selected in the second and third rounds, plus any undrafted rookies signed to training camp deals, will be paid $270,000.It doesn’t mean all will make rosters, but the changes do mean more opportunity than ever before. The fit is still the most important. Te-Hina Paopao, a national champion with South Carolina, waited until No. 18 overall a year ago, but settled into a starting role with the Atlanta Dream by the playoffs. Kaitlyn Chen, the No. 30 pick, averaged 10 minutes per game for Golden State, the league’s highest-attended franchise in its first expansion year.AdvertisementSouth Carolina’s trio of drafteesWNBA teams have become increasingly willing to take fliers on South Carolina players, as they often have with UConn players. Of the 12 players on training camp rosters last year, nine stuck for opening day.That was third behind UConn (15) and Notre Dame (12). UConn’s potential draftees consist of lottery pick Fudd and transfer forward Serah Williams. Notre Dame could be represented by Cassandre Prosper, a Canadian native who declared early for the draft.Raven Johnson and Ta'Niya Latson are likely to become just the latest Gamecocks to make their marks in the WNBA. (Photo by Jacob Kupferman/Getty Images) (Jacob Kupferman via Getty Images)There are three Gamecocks in a good position to hear their name called in the first round on Monday.Ta’Niya Latson, a 5-9 guard, led Division I in scoring as a junior at Florida State before transferring to the Gamecocks in hopes of winning a national championship and further developing for the pro game. Alongside all-SEC and All-American players, Latson had her most efficient college season (48.6 FG%, 52.2 eFG%) and most productive (1.15 points per scoring attempt).AdvertisementRaven Johnson is an elite old-school ball-handler who became a rare SEC Defensive Player of the Year as the perimeter leader of the Gamecocks’ “seatbelt gang.” Ranked opponents shot 38.4% with the 5-9 point guard on the court compared to 42.4% off during the regular season, per South Carolina, and she limited UConn All-Americans Sarah Strong and Azzi Fudd in the Final Four.“They are well-rounded individuals from a basketball standpoint,” South Carolina head coach Dawn Staley said after losing the national title game in Phoenix. “They are great humans. You want somebody in your franchise that you see that's going to come to work every day on time, early, come in early, stay late, then everything in between.”Madina Okot, a 6-6 center, will also hear her name called after the NCAA denied South Carolina’s petition to the NCAA for an extra year of eligibility. Okot, a Kenyan native, began playing basketball in 2020 and played two seasons for Zetech University in Kenya while awaiting approval of multiple U.S. visa attempts. Her fifth was approved, and she played one year at Mississippi State before transferring to South Carolina.Okot is dominant in the post (71.4% at the rim) with an emerging shooter’s touch. She was 13 of 29 from the perimeter after zero attempts a year ago.AdvertisementUCLA’s record-setting night?Expect to hear a lot of talk about the national champions on Monday. UCLA’s winning six are all on draft boards. If they are all taken, the program would set the record for most players drafted in a single night.Tennessee, Notre Dame and South Carolina all sent five players to the WNBA in a single draft at least once. The Lady Vols did it twice. All four times it happened, the No. 1 overall pick was from said program.UCLA could set a record for most players drafted in one night. (Photo by Greg Fiore/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)Lauren Betts, UCLA’s 6-7 center, is a projected lottery pick unlikely to go No. 1 unless there’s draft movement. Her physique is a major asset to WNBA front offices, and she improved her stock with a strong final NCAA tournament that concluded with the title and Most Outstanding Player honor.AdvertisementShe averaged 21 points, 9.3 rebounds, 3.2 assists and 2.8 blocks over six games and shot at least 60% from the field in every one. It’s her versatility and abilities on the defensive end that shine brightest.Gianna Kneepkens is one of the draft’s best perimeter shooters, first at Utah and last season at UCLA. The 6-foot guard is 43% from 3-point range in her career. Gabriela Jaquez, a 6-foot shooting guard, arguably could have been named the Final Four’s MOP and touched career-highs in scoring (13.5 ppg), steals (1.1), field goal percentage (53.9%) and 3-point percentage (39%).Kiki Rice, a 5-11 point guard, also put up career highs her senior year. The former No. 2 recruit in the 2022 class is best when she’s getting downhill. Charlisse Leger-Walker, who turns 25 in September, and Angela Dugalić, a 6-4 forward who played with the Serbian national team at EuroBasket qualifiers, are fringe first-rounders.The mass number of UCLA draftees could become more of the norm in the transfer portal era, which is heading toward super-team building.AdvertisementWNBA draft names to watch Flau’jae Johnson, a four-year starter at LSU, didn’t boost her draft stock in an NCAA tournament run that ended short of the Elite Eight. She was inconsistent in college and never developed as deeply as she should have after a standout national championship freshman year. Yet, she’s still a high-ceiling player who can score. She could go anywhere from first after the lottery to the end of the first.On the outside is Rori Harmon, a fifth-year point guard who trails a more well-rounded, productive package of Miles or Rice, or even Kentucky’s Tonie Morgan. She’s undersized at 5-6, the same height as only four players in the W a year ago (Aari McDonald, Dana Evans, Jordin Canada, Moriah Jefferson).Her defensive tenacity and basketball IQ could keep her around a roster, which likely wouldn’t have been the case if she had come out a year ago with fewer availability spots.Advertisement“If you want somebody that's going to set the tone, is going to bring it every day, don't care if you're a 12-year vet or a rookie, I'm going to guard your ass, you go get her because she's good,” Texas head coach Vic Schaefer said. “She can run a team. That's the thing at that level, you got to have somebody that can run the team.”Ole Miss forward Cotie McMahon, a transfer from Ohio State, is a fringe first-rounder who plays a physical style that would translate to the pros. Richmond forward Maggie Doogan could become the first Richmond player drafted after her stock rose throughout another consistently productive season.The three rounds will be filled with international players beyond Fam. They are often draft-and-stash opportunities for franchises to hold a player’s rights and bring them into the fold when a player is ready, or when the franchise has a need and spot.
